verses.text: Guard your steps when you go to God’s house; for to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they don’t know that they do evil.
Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.
For as a dream comes with a multitude of cares, so a fool’s speech with a multitude of words.
When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow.
It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay.
Don’t allow your mouth to lead you into sin. Don’t protest before the messenger that this was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice, and destroy the work of your hands?
For in the multitude of dreams there are vanities, as well as in many words: but you must fear God.

If you see the oppression of the poor, and the violent taking away of justice and righteousness in a district, don’t marvel at the matter: for one official is eyed by a higher one; and there are officials over them.
Moreover the profit of the earth is for all. The king profits from the field.
He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.
When goods increase, those who eat them are increased; and what advantage is there to its owner, except to feast on them with his eyes?
The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, whether he eats little or much; but the abundance of the rich will not allow him to sleep.
There is a grievous evil which I have seen under the sun: wealth kept by its owner to his harm.
Those riches perish by misfortune, and if he has fathered a son, there is nothing in his hand.
As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.
This also is a grievous evil, that in all points as he came, so shall he go. And what profit does he have who labors for the wind?
All his days he also eats in darkness, he is frustrated, and has sickness and wrath.

Behold, that which I have seen to be good and proper is for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy good in all his labor, in which he labors under the sun, all the days of his life which God has given him; for this is his portion.
Every man also to whom God has given riches and wealth, and has given him power to eat of it, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labor — this is the gift of God.
For he shall not often reflect on the days of his life; because God occupies him with the joy of his heart.

footnotes.content: We approach the temple — or any place of prayer — with so much chatter in our heads. But the Preacher says the real act is listening, not talking. I've learned that worship is often best when I come quiet, ready to hear what the Lord wants to say to me, not just to bend His ear with my noise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's a beautiful geometry in this: God in heaven, us on earth — a vast distance that makes silence our wisdom. When we stand before the Holy One, fewer words let Him be heard. I think of Martha in Luke's house, fussing, while Mary sat at Jesus' feet listening — the Preacher knew which was better.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A fool's many words tumble like fragments of a restless dream — each one pulling at the next, and none of them real. I notice this in myself when I'm anxious: the more I talk, the less sense I make. Rest, not more speech, is what steadies a wandering heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A vow is not a light thing. When we promise God something, we're no longer in the realm of wishes or half-thoughts — we've made a covenant with Him. The delay in paying is its own kind of sin, as if we think He'll forget, or won't hold us to our word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Better to say nothing than to say yes and then turn away. There's mercy in silence, but there's judgment in a broken promise. I've watched people vow and falter, and I've seen how it hardens something in them, a small unfaithfulness that spreads.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Preacher sees a soul scrambling to excuse itself, stammering before God's messenger. But excuses are wind — they don't pay the debt, and they only multiply the sin. Better to repent than to explain away what we owe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dreams, chatter, schemes — they all amount to nothing. Yet one thread runs through all of it: fear of God. That one truth, held fast, keeps us honest. It's not the fear of judgment alone, but the fear that comes from loving Him and not wanting to disappoint Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Preacher looks at the poor man robbed of justice by a chain of corrupt officials, each one watching the one above. Don't be surprised, he says. Corruption runs deep. But this isn't cynicism — it's a call to remember that God sees what happens in every district, at every level.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The earth yields its increase for all — the soil is generous, the harvest shared. Even the king must eat from the field like everyone else. There's something humbling in this: we are all dependent on the same ground, the same rain, the same grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The love of silver is a thirst that grows with every drink. I've seen men chase wealth thinking the next sum will satisfy them — and it never does. The Preacher names it plainly: vanity. Only love of God can fill the place where that hunger lives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: More goods mean more mouths to feed and more hands reaching out. And the owner? He stands there watching his possessions like a man watching a show he can't enjoy. He owns it all and owns nothing of its peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The laboring man, whether his belly is full or empty, sleeps the sleep of the just. But the rich man, surrounded by abundance, lies awake — his mind churning over how to keep it, how to grow it. The Preacher knows which man has true rest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wealth hoarded becomes a curse. The Preacher calls it a grievous evil — not the wealth itself, but the keeping of it, the clutching, the refusal to let it flow. God's gifts are meant to move through our hands, not to be locked in them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One misfortune, and the wealth is gone. A man worked his whole life to build it, only to watch it scatter like leaves. His son inherits nothing but the memory of what was lost. This is why the Preacher keeps saying: vanity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We came naked from the womb and we'll leave the same way — that's the one unchangeable fact. All our labor, all our earning, all our scheming to pile up what we can carry — none of it goes with us. This verse strips away pretense. We own nothing, really.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He labors for the wind — working hard, accumulating, dying empty-handed, just as he came. The Preacher sees the grim symmetry and asks the hard question: what profit? What good is a life spent chasing what we cannot keep? Only Jesus answers that question with love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All his days in darkness, frustrated, sick at heart. This is the man who serves his own greed instead of serving God. The Preacher doesn't soften it — he calls it what it is. Sin and selfishness have a taste, and it is bitter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After all his warnings, the Preacher lands on this — it is good and proper to eat, drink, and enjoy the fruit of your labor. This is not indulgence; it's gratitude. The gift is not the wealth, but the chance to work, to eat what you've grown, to be satisfied and know it's enough. This is the road back to contentment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God gives riches and the power to enjoy them — that's the real blessing, not the gold itself. To have much and to rejoice in your labor, to see your work and be glad — this is what makes a rich man. The poor man with a grateful heart is richer still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He doesn't often brood on his days because God keeps him occupied with joy — not with tasks, but with the quiet gladness of a heart that trusts. Readers today hear an echo in this: when we're held in God's joy, the weight of counting our years, our worth, our losses, somehow lifts. We're too busy being grateful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
